 Doctors warn of the fever-reducing trap in dengue fever patients.
 According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, dengue fever patients can enter the critical phase from the 3rd to the 7th day, even if the fever has subsided and the body shows signs of recovery.
 Người Đưa Tin • 11/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 The National Hospital for Tropical Diseases has just reported on two female patients, aged 23 and 53, who developed severe dengue fever with significantly reduced platelet counts, elevated liver enzymes (nearly 2,000 U/L), along with coagulation disorders and organ damage. Notably, the disease can worsen even when the patient's fever begins to subside.
 Specifically, the first patient is BH (53 years old, Hai Phong), who was previously healthy and had never had dengue fever. After 5 days of continuous high fever, sometimes reaching 39-40 degrees Celsius, accompanied by general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain, the patient went to a medical facility and was diagnosed with Dengue virus infection.
 Test results showed a rapid drop in platelet count from 38 to 21 G/L. Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, platelet count was 23 G/L, AST was elevated to 1,939 U/L, ALT was 804 U/L, accompanied by coagulation disorders and subcutaneous bleeding. The patient was diagnosed with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever with liver damage.
 The second case is PL (23 years old, Hanoi ). After 7 days of intermittent high fever, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and loose stools, her condition did not improve despite prior treatment at a medical facility.
 Laboratory tests revealed a platelet count of 21 G/L, elevated AST of 1,907 U/L, and ALT of 883 U/L. Ultrasound detected fluid in the abdominal cavity and both pleural spaces, suggesting plasma leakage. This is a dangerous complication that can lead to hypovolemia and shock if not treated promptly. 
 Many dengue fever patients are being treated at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases (Photo: Provided by the hospital).
 You may also like Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 16 dengue fever patients, including some severe cases requiring close monitoring.
 According to MSc. Dr. Pham Van Phuc - Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit, Dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the Dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can occur at all ages, including those who were previously completely healthy.
 According to Dr. Phuc , thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but the severity of the disease cannot be assessed solely based on platelet count. The risk of complications needs to be evaluated holistically based on clinical condition and many other indicators such as signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and signs of organ damage.
 "In these two cases, in addition to a sharp drop in platelets, the patients also had very high liver enzymes, blood clotting disorders, and other warning signs. These abnormalities indicate that the disease has progressed seriously and requires close monitoring to detect and treat complications promptly," Dr. Phuc said.
 In particular, one of the key points to note about dengue fever is that the disease can worsen when the patient's fever begins to subside. The dangerous phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day of the illness when the patient may experience plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage.
 If not detected and treated promptly, severe plasma leakage can lead to hypovolemia, shock, multiple organ failure, and be life-threatening.
 Dr. Phuc emphasized that patients and their families should not assess the severity of the illness based solely on body temperature. A reduction in fever does not necessarily mean the illness has passed the critical stage.
 People who have or suspect they have dengue fever should go to a medical facility immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy or restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue.
 You may also like If a doctor instructs the patient to monitor and treat the condition at home, the patient should rest, stay adequately hydrated, monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Do not increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a doctor's prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue fever.
 Attending scheduled follow-up appointments, undergoing prescribed tests, and closely monitoring the patient during the 3rd to 7th day are crucial for early detection of the risk of worsening condition. Patients should not be complacent when their fever subsides or symptoms seem to improve, as this could be the time when the disease enters a dangerous stage.
 To proactively prevent dengue fever, people need to implement several measures simultaneously, such as eliminating stagnant water sources, destroying mosquito larvae, limiting mosquito bites, and maintaining a clean living environment. In addition, dengue vaccination is a proactive preventive measure that people can choose according to the instructions of healthcare workers and the regulations of vaccination centers.
 However, vaccination does not replace mosquito control measures and prevention of mosquito bites. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, people should still go to a medical facility for examination, testing, and appropriate monitoring guidance.
